units: the writer is writing from a room fitted out under the roof
the roof had been letting water in since the cold season
the water that seeped in warped the beams
the warping of the timber stopped the landing door from closing
the craftsman took the leaf off and trimmed the jamb
two lengths of the roof frame were strengthened
the writer invites the person he is writing to to sleep in this room
the room is not heated yet
text: I am writing to you from the little room under the roof, the one we called the loft when we were small. Since the cold months the covering had been letting water through, and that seeping swelled the beams until they twisted out of true. The carpenter was blunt about it. Once timber shifts, the landing door stops closing; its hinge pulled crooked and the frame went out of square. He took the leaf off, planed the jamb back, then hung the whole thing again. Two rafters were doubled up as well, since the roof load was sitting badly. The result pleases me. The pitch runs clean, resin smells right through the stairwell, and you can hear the rain without dreading it. The upstairs room is yours whenever you come. Bring thick sheets, though, because the heating does not reach it yet, and the view over the valley is worth that chill.

units: an old wall is not rendered like a recent wall
the professional compares the old wall to something that breathes
a waterproof render traps the water coming up from below ground
this trapped water brings salt deposits to the surface
the render ends up coming away in pieces
lime laid on in thin coats lets the vapour out
a surface that is too smooth must be rubbed down and wetted before rendering
this method slows the work down but keeps the wall from decaying
text: Should a wall of some age be rendered exactly the way a recent one is? The site manager we put the question to says no, and his answer turns on a single image: the old wall breathes, the young one sweats. What happens if you seal the first of them under a waterproof mortar? Damp drawn up from below stays shut in, salt blooms at the surface, the coat blisters and comes away in sheets. What does he offer instead? Lime, laid on in thin passes, so that the masonry can let its vapour out. And if the backing proves too smooth for that? Rub it down, he says, wet it thoroughly, then throw on a very loose first pass that will grip. Work goes more slowly that way, he grants, but the wall stops rotting quietly behind its skin. A front treated so will stand a whole generation before it needs doing again.

units: the foreman asks the craftsman how the floor should be fixed down
a nail goes in quickly
a nail bends without snapping under shaking
a screw holds better when something pulls on it
a screw shears if the structure moves
laying a heavy piece over joists calls for a fixing that tolerates the timber moving
a screw costs more in tools and in care
the parts meant to come apart again will be screwed down
text: The site foreman asks the joiner whether the boards of the upper floor ought to be nailed down or screwed. Nails go in fast, the joiner says, and they take knocks well, because the shank bends rather than snapping under the shaking. A screw holds far better against pull, he adds, but it shears clean off once the frame moves under load. A heavy board laid over joists needs a fixing that tolerates timber shrinking and swelling. The foreman weighs up the cost of the two methods. A screw wants a power tool and a careful hand; a nail wants a hammer and a steady rhythm. So you nail the layers that swell and shrink, the joiner concludes, and you screw down whatever you may want to lift again later. On this job, he adds, the battens go down with nails and the inspection hatches with screws.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: three great methods came before the general use of metal
the first method piles stones on one another without mortar
the steadiness of that pile comes from the weight of the blocks
the second method uses clay bricks dried without firing
the third method combines a frame and an infill covered with plaster
each way of building depended on the materials lying close by
these ways of building forced thick walls and low buildings
villages built this way are still lived in and still kept up the same way
text: Before metal came into general use, the builder's craft rested on three families of method. The first stacks chosen blocks of stone with nothing binding them, and draws its steadiness from the sheer weight of each course. The second shapes raw clay into bricks dried in the open air, bedded in a mud of the same stuff. The third raises a timber frame, packs it with a light infill, then has the whole face plastered over. Each answered to what lay close at hand: outcropping rock, river silt, the wood of a nearby forest. Each imposed its limits too, modest heights, thick walls, constant upkeep. Builders made up for that by turning the openings to the light, deepening the footings and steepening the roofs. Their legacy survives in whole hamlets, lived in still, where repairs are made with the old gestures.

units: the stages of a building job follow an order that cannot be changed
a plank fence marks the limits of the plot at the start
the footings are poured into trenches dug in the ground
the walls rise with gaps left for the doors and windows
the roof frame goes up once the masonry has dried
the covering puts the job under shelter from the rain
the pipes run through the partitions while these are still open
a render laid on a damp backing comes away
text: Nothing on a plot being made ready for a house is placed at random, since every stage sets up the one that follows. The ground is first marked out with a plank fence, which shields the disturbed soil and gives the machines their bearings. Trenches are then dug for the footings and filled with reinforced concrete. Walls rise course by course, with gaps left where doors and windows will sit. The roof frame goes up once the masonry has hardened, and the covering closes the volume, putting the work under shelter. Water and air pipes run through the partitions while these are still open. Rendering comes last, then floors, then paint. Swapping any two of these stages proves expensive: a coat laid on a damp wall lifts off, and a partition closed too early has to be opened again.

units: a lock that jammed set the whole business going
the occupants forced the door while joking about it
one push that was too rough tore the metal part out of the frame
the bottom hinge gave way under the weight of the leaf
the door dropped down and scraped along the tiles
the caretaker wanted to replace the lot
a resident who restores furniture was given time to try the repair
she took the door off and knocked the frame back true
the neighbour earned a name in the building as a woodworker
text: It all started with a sticky lock in the basement of our block. At first we shoved a bit harder, we laughed about it, we said the door had character. Then a neighbour pushed too roughly: the keep tore out of the frame and the bottom hinge ripped away. The leaf being heavy, it dropped sideways and scraped along the tiles for its whole swing. Nothing moved after that, and nobody dared force it. The caretaker wanted the lot replaced, quote in hand, but the tenant on the ground floor, who restores furniture, asked for a week. She lifted the leaf off its pins, knocked the frame back true with a mallet, fitted a fresh hinge and greased the mechanism. The lock has snapped shut ever since. That repair earned her a name across the building as a cabinetmaker, which she had never gone looking for.

units: an opening that rubs makes a room unpleasant to use
the cause is seldom in the glass
rubbing low down points to the timber having swollen
rubbing high up points to the fixings having worked loose
the shiny patch left by the contact has to be sanded
a light oil is then wiped on and left overnight
the brackets are screwed back with the holes shifted slightly
a level set on the sill lets you check that the frame stands upright
a thin packer corrects a frame that is still twisted
text: A window that sticks spoils the use of a whole room, and the fault seldom lies in the glass itself. Start by watching the gap: rubbing low down means the timber has swollen, rubbing high up means the fixing brackets have worked loose. In the first case, open the casement fully, find the shiny band left by the contact, and sand that strip down with a medium paper until it swings clear again. Dust it off, wipe on a light oil, and leave it overnight. In the second, the brackets must be screwed back, with the holes shifted a little so the screws bite sound wood. Then check that the frame stands upright, with a spirit level set on the inner sill. Should the frame still sit twisted, slip a thin packer behind the top hinge. Adjusting it patiently spares you a costly replacement.

units: two building jobs are going on facing each other
one of them is a tall block of flats
the balconies of that block arrive ready made
lifting machines set whole face panels in place
that block gains one storey a week
the other job is the putting right of an old house
the men there take the roof covering off piece by piece
they check the state of the walls and change the timber that has gone
the neighbours like the room they are promised but hold to the front being restored
text: Two building sites face each other along one street, and nothing links them but the dust. On one side a block of flats climbs, its balconies arriving from the works already moulded, with their rounded lip and all. Cranes set whole face panels down, and the front gains a storey a week. Opposite, an old house lies open like a patient on a table: the men lift the tiles off one by one, sound the masonry, replace the dead lengths of the roof frame. Where the first site glories in speed, the second keeps faith with the way joints were once made. People living nearby watch both and cannot choose. They admire the room the tall block promises, yet they cling to the scaffolding on the old front, which will give them back a street they thought lost. Neither, in their eyes, is pointless.

units: the frame carrying the building can be seen from outside
the upright posts were cut to shape with a hand tool
each post carries a horizontal piece that takes the roof frame
the walls are made of three layers one over another
a flow of air is left within the thickness of the walls
the windows have a sloping sill that throws the water off
the ground around the building is covered with draining stones
the overhang of the roof keeps the timber out of the weather
no surface has been painted
text: Seen from the yard, the shed shows its frame before anything else about it. The timber posts, squared off with an axe on all four faces, each carry a horizontal beam that takes the trusses. The walls are built up in three layers: an overlapping board skin outside, a ventilated air gap, an insulating panel fixed onto battens from within. The openings follow one pattern, a low apron below, a jutting sill cut on the slant to throw water off, a lintel in a single piece. The floor pairs a smooth slab inside with a band of draining gravel laid along the walls outside. The roof, pitched both ways, ends in a wide overhang that keeps the rain off the woodwork. Nothing has been painted: the boarding greys, the ironwork takes on a patina, and the whole thing ages without heavy upkeep.

units: building has slowly given up on lasting a long time
supple mortars were replaced by a harder binder
that binder was taken up because it sets quickly
heavy roof frames gave way to lightened structures
those lightened structures cannot be mended and have to be replaced
thick coatings were replaced by very thin layers
the guarantee on those coatings runs out before the wall wears
each of these choices was aimed at saving money in the short term
the writer calls for materials that can be mended
text: We have given up building to last, and the drift set in by stages. Masons first dropped the supple binders in favour of a stiff cement of their own, quicker to set and easier to bring to the site. Heavy roof frames then gave way to light trusses, calculated to the bone, which nobody can mend except by putting in fresh ones. Thick renders gave way at last to films so thin that their guarantee runs out long before the wall behind them tires. Every one of these stages was defended by an immediate saving; taken together they leave a stock of buildings that will have to come down before they can ever grow old with dignity. A building worth the name takes repair after repair. To ask for materials that can be mended is not a builder's nostalgia at all: it is ordinary prudence.
